Orientation: Two Lectures, One Question

This week pairs two very different voices on the same subject, and the exam will draw from both.

🖐️

Dr. Sendzicki — The Model & The Hands

Teaches Sutherland's cranial concept as a working clinical model: what the Primary Respiratory Mechanism is, its five components, the vocabulary of flexion/extension, how to hold a head, what you may and may not treat, and the specific lab techniques.

  • This is the testable framework — memorize the five principles, the motion pairs, and the contraindications.
📈

Dr. Willard — The Data

An anatomist who has, by his own statement, never palpated any of these rhythms — deliberately, so he can look at the recordings without defending a technique. He shows what is actually measurable: real low-frequency oscillations in blood flow that trained hands can follow and that treatment demonstrably changes.

  • This is the evidence layer — it supports that a rhythm exists and is palpable, while questioning the explanation attached to it.
🔑 The one idea that ties the week together — data vs. hypothesis

Data is what you collect: it should be objective and reproducible. Hypothesis is the story you build on top of the data. Willard's warning is that in every scientific field — osteopathy is not remotely unique here — the hypothesis becomes the practitioner's "child," gets defended, and eventually people fight over the story while ignoring the numbers.

Applied to this week: "a rhythmic, palpable change in the head" is the data. "The cranial bones are moving because the brain coils and uncoils" is one hypothesis. "You are feeling vascular pulsation in a dense venous plexus" is another. You are allowed to learn the model, use it clinically, and still keep the two categories separate.

🧬 Willard's illustration — Golgi vs. Cajal, 1906

Camillo Golgi (Italy, inventor of the silver stain) and Santiago Ramón y Cajal (Spain, who used Golgi's stain better than Golgi did) looked at the same slides, from the same species, prepared with the same technique — and reached opposite conclusions. Golgi said the nervous system was one continuous network joined by cytoplasmic bridges; Cajal said neurons were separate cells communicating across gaps (which he romantically called "protoplasmic kisses" — what we now call synapses).

They shared the 1906 Nobel Prize and would not speak to each other. Cajal died believing he had won. Then the electron microscope arrived — and it turns out many neurons are joined by cytoplasmic bridges, the gap junctions. Same data, opposite hypotheses, and the truth sat in the middle.

🩺 Who was Sutherland?

William Garner Sutherland, DO (1873–1954) — a student of A.T. Still. From research and observation he concluded that the central nervous system, cerebrospinal fluid, dural membranes, cranial bones, and sacrum function as a single unit exhibiting cyclic motion. He published The Cranial Bowl in 1939. He framed the cranial concept as an extension of Still's principle that "all parts of the whole body obey the one eternal law of life and motion" — and he kept revising the model his whole life.

Q: A question stem describes "the integrated model of cyclic inhalation and exhalation involving the brain, cerebrospinal fluid, membranes, cranial bones, and sacrum." Which term is being defined, and who described it?

Answer

The Primary Respiratory Mechanism (PRM), described by William Garner Sutherland, DO (The Cranial Bowl, 1939). Do not confuse the PRM with its palpable output, the Cranial Rhythmic Impulse (CRI) — the PRM is the mechanism, the CRI is the rhythm you feel.

LO 1 — Major Biorhythms of the Body

Identify & Distinguish

The Body's Nested Rhythms: Heart, Breath, and the CRI

Every biological system, from the nucleus up to the whole organism, runs on rhythms. The osteopathic question is narrower: which of them are slow enough and strong enough that a human hand can count them? Three matter for this objective.

RhythmRateFrequency (cycles/second)DriverHow you detect it
Cardiac (heart rate)~60–100 beats/min~0.9 cpsSinoatrial node; intrinsic cardiac pacemakingRadial pulse, auscultation, ECG
Diaphragmatic respiration12–18 breaths/min0.2–0.3 cpsBrainstem respiratory centers driving the diaphragmWatch/feel chest and abdominal excursion
Cranial Rhythmic Impulse (CRI)10–14 cycles/min (taught value, healthy adult)~0.17–0.23 cpsThe five components of the PRM acting togetherPalpation — vault, base, or A-P hold
Baroreflex / Traube-Hering-Mayer wave5–8 cycles/min~0.1 cpsSympathetic tone cycling on the baroreceptor reflexLaser-Doppler flowmetry (and, per Nelson & Glonek, palpation)
Very-low-frequency wave< 1 cycle/min0.02–0.05 cpsThermal regulation and/or renin-angiotensin releaseLaser-Doppler flowmetry with Fourier analysis
⚠️ The number conflict you must be able to hold in your head

Sendzicki teaches the classic Sutherland/Magoun figure: the CRI is 10–14 cycles per minute in a normal healthy adult. Willard presents laser-Doppler data in which what skilled palpators are actually tracking is the 5–8 cycles per minute baroreflex (Traube-Hering-Mayer) wave.

For a rate question, answer 10–14 cycles/minute. For a "what is the CRI physiologically related to / what did the flowmetry study show" question, answer the Traube-Hering-Mayer oscillation at 5–8 cycles/minute. Both are examinable; they come from different lectures.

What speeds the CRI up and what slows it down

⏫

CRI Accelerated

  • Fever
  • Vigorous exercise
  • After OMT (osteopathic manipulative treatment) directed at the PRM — i.e. a successful treatment response
⏬

CRI Decelerated

  • Depression
  • Stress — physical or emotional
  • Chronic fatigue
  • Chronic infection

Why rhythms sit inside other rhythms — the physics, briefly

Willard builds this from a spring with a weight on it. The weight stretches the spring until the stiffness of the steel reverses the motion; the spring lifts until the weight reverses it again. Those two limits are the boundary conditions, and they set the amplitude (how far the wave swings from the midline — a measure of the energy in the system) and the frequency (the distance between the same point on two successive waves).

  1. One boundary pair = one clean oscillation. A fixed spring in a fixed room gives you a single, regular wave.
  2. Move the boundaries and the wave gets a second, slower rhythm. Put the spring in a box and cycle the temperature: warm makes the steel more compliant and the swing bigger, cold damps it. Now the amplitude of the fast wave rises and falls on a slow cycle.
  3. Cycle the temperature control itself and you get a third layer — a boundary on the boundary on the boundary.
  4. A living body is this, several layers deep. Multiple regulatory systems, each with its own period, each modulating the ones beneath it. That is why a real recording looks like a fast wave whose height and spacing keep changing.
🧠 Why the rhythm sometimes disappears under your hands

When several oscillations of different periods are superimposed, they drift in and out of phase. Where peaks line up, the combined wave gets large. Where a peak of one lands on a trough of another, they cancel and the combined amplitude can fall below the threshold you can palpate — then rise again as they drift back out of phase.

Palpators call that flat interval a still point. On the flowmetry tracings, examiners reliably said "I'm losing it" exactly where the recorded wave collapsed in amplitude — and picked it up again when it returned. This is a purely physical explanation for a phenomenon usually described in more mystical terms.

How the rhythms are actually recorded

Laser-Doppler Flowmetry

Clip on a skin fold — the earlobe works well

A laser beam passes through the skin fold and is read on the far side. It is sensitive enough to detect the compaction of red blood cells in the capillaries during systole and their slight rarefaction (spreading apart) during diastole. Output: a continuous cutaneous blood-flow-velocity tracing.

Band-Pass Filtering

Computer removes the fast "chatter"

The raw trace is dominated by the ~1-per-second cardiac spike, which visually buries everything slower. Filtering out that band leaves the long, slow waves visible on their own.

Fourier Transformation → Power Spectrum

Converts a time record into a frequency record

The x-axis is no longer time — it is events per second (frequency). The y-axis height is power, the amount of energy present at that frequency. A tall peak at 0.9 cps means "a lot of the energy in this recording is happening about once a second" — the heartbeat.

⚠️ The single most common misread of a power spectrum

Students look at the x-axis and assume it is time, because the tracing above it was a time record. It is not. On a power spectrum the x-axis is frequency (events per second) and the y-axis is power (energy at that frequency). A peak's height tells you how much of the signal's energy lives at that rate — not how big any single beat was.

The four long cardiovascular waves — read this figure

Figure — the four long cardiovascular waves (after Glonek; Willard slides 23–24). Note the baroreflex peak is the one palpators track.

🩺 Where each wave comes from, physiologically
  • Cardiac (~0.9 cps): the intrinsic beat itself — the fundamental wave everything else rides on.
  • Respiratory (0.2–0.3 cps): breathing changes intrathoracic pressure, which changes cardiac filling and therefore heart rate. The heart rate oscillates up and down 12–18 times a minute. (This is respiratory sinus arrhythmia.)
  • Baroreflex (0.1 cps): the sympathoadrenal system raising and lowering vascular tone. Baroreceptors sense pressure, heart rate and vessel tone are adjusted, pressure overshoots, and the loop cycles at roughly 5–8 times a minute. Because several autonomic subsystems drift semi-independently, this band is itself complex — hence the compound name Traube-Hering-Mayer (Traube and Hering described components in the late 1800s with primitive instruments; Mayer added another).
  • Very low frequency (<1 cpm): attributed to thermal regulation and/or periodic renin–angiotensin release, imposing a slow overall rise and fall across everything above it.

Q: On a Fourier power spectrum of cutaneous blood-flow velocity, a distinct peak appears at approximately 0.1 cycles per second. What physiologic oscillation does this represent, and why is it osteopathically relevant?

Answer

It is the baroreflex wave — the Traube-Hering-Mayer oscillation, roughly 5–8 cycles per minute, generated by sympathetic (sympathoadrenal) cycling of vascular tone on the baroreceptor reflex loop. It is osteopathically relevant because in the Nelson & Glonek laser-Doppler studies, this is the wave that trained examiners were actually tracking when they called out the Cranial Rhythmic Impulse, and it is the wave whose power changed measurably with cranial treatment.

LO 2 — Define the Primary Respiratory Mechanism

Core Definition

The Primary Respiratory Mechanism (PRM)

🔑 Definition — memorize this shape

The Primary Respiratory Mechanism (PRM) is Sutherland's model describing an integrated set of five anatomic-physiologic components — the central nervous system, the cerebrospinal fluid, the dural membranes, the cranial bones, and the sacrum — whose development and function are synchronous and interdependent, and which together produce a cyclic motion expressed as inhalation and exhalation throughout the cranium and body.

These five components are also called the five phenomena of the PRM.

🧠 Why "primary" and why "respiratory"?
  • Respiratory — because its two phases are named inhalation and exhalation, and because the cycle represents a dynamic metabolic interchange (fluid exchange, tissue perfusion) throughout the body, not just air movement.
  • Primary — because in Sutherland's framing this cycle is more fundamental than the thoracic breath. Thoracic breathing is secondary respiration; the PRM is the deeper, inherent cycle present from embryologic development.
  • The cranial concept is presented as a model of integrated structure and physiologic function, consistent with A.T. Still's principle that all parts of the body obey one law of life and motion. Sutherland himself kept modifying the model across his career — it was never presented as finished.

PRM vs. CRI — do not conflate these

⚙️

PRM = the mechanism

The five integrated anatomic-physiologic components themselves. A model of what is moving and why. You do not palpate "the PRM" — you palpate its output.

👋

CRI = the palpable rhythm

The two-phase rhythmic cycle (inhalation/exhalation) that results from the synchronous, interdependent motion of the five PRM components, felt throughout the body. 10–14 cycles/minute in a normal healthy adult.

The two phases and what each one means everywhere in the body

StructureINHALATION phase (= flexion)EXHALATION phase (= extension)
Central nervous systemCoils forward; shortens and thickensUncoils; lengthens and thins
Midline cranial bones
(occiput, sphenoid, ethmoid, vomer)		Flexion about transverse axesExtension about transverse axes
Paired / lateral bones
(temporal, parietal, frontal, mandible, facial)		External rotationInternal rotation
Sphenobasilar synchondrosis (SBS)RisesFalls
Cranial vaultLowersRises
Skull shapeAnterior-posterior diameter decreases; skull widensAnterior-posterior diameter increases; skull narrows
Sacrum (midline structure)COUNTERnutation — base posterior, apex anteriorNUTATION — base anterior, apex posterior
⚠️ The classic trap — sacral nutation is "backwards" here

In the postural/respiratory model you learned earlier, sacral nutation (base anterior) pairs with inhalation of the thoracic breath. In the PRM, it is the opposite: PRM inhalation/flexion = counternutation (sacral base posterior), and PRM exhalation/extension = nutation (sacral base anterior).

Memory hook: in cranial inhalation the whole mechanism shortens and widens — the occiput rocks so the sacral base is pulled back. Read the stem carefully for whether it says "primary respiratory mechanism" or "thoracic/postural respiration."

Picture the shape change

Figure — "The head is a modified sphere." Three-dimensional shape change across the two phases of the PRM.

Slide 12 — superior (top-down) view: the skull in extreme extension (left, long and narrow) vs. extreme flexion (right, short and wide). Dashed line is the neutral outline.

Slide 13 — the transverse axes of the midline bones: ethmoidal, sphenoidal, occipital, and vomer. These are the bones that flex and extend; everything paired rotates instead.

Q: During the inhalation phase of the Primary Respiratory Mechanism, the temporal bones and the sacrum do what?

Answer

The temporal bones externally rotate (they are paired/lateral structures, so they rotate rather than flex), and the sacrum counternutates — sacral base moves posteriorly, apex anteriorly, about the superior transverse axis at S2. Simultaneously the sphenobasilar synchondrosis rises, the vault lowers, and the skull widens as its anterior-posterior diameter decreases.

LO 3 — Describe the Reciprocal Tension Membrane

Membranous Anatomy

The Reciprocal Tension Membrane (RTM)

🔑 Definition

The Reciprocal Tension Membrane (RTM) is the intracranial and intraspinal membrane system — the meninges, functionally meaning the dura — that surrounds, supports, and partitions the central nervous system. Because the dura is tough, fibrous, inelastic, and firmly attached to the cranial bones, motion in the membrane is transmitted to the bones. Dural tension regulates the movement of the cranial bones — the tension in one part is reciprocally balanced against the tension in another, which is where the name comes from.

Slide 10 — the Reciprocal Tension Membrane: the falx (vertical, midline) and the tentorium (horizontal, tent-shaped) seen inside a sectioned skull.

Dural anatomy the objective actually asks for

  • The meninges have three layers: dura mater (outermost, tough), arachnoid mater (middle, web-like), and pia mater (innermost, adherent to brain surface).
  • The dura is the only true connective tissue in the cranium. This is why cranial dysfunction is described as a membranous problem, not a joint problem.
  • The cranial dura has two layers. The outer layer is continuous with the inner periosteum of the skull bones, and continuous with the outer periosteum through the sutures. Developmentally, this continuity means each cranial bone effectively sits inside its own membranous bag.
  • The two dural layers are inseparable except where they split to form the venous (dural) sinuses — superior sagittal, transverse, sigmoid, straight, cavernous, occipital.
  • The dura projects caudally down the spinal canal with firm attachments at the foramen magnum, C2, C3, and S2. Memorize: FM · C2 · C3 · S2
  • Inherent motion of the brain and spinal cord, plus fluctuation of the cerebrospinal fluid, moves the membranes; the membranes then move the bones.

Slide 11 — the dural tube drawn end to end. Note the firm dural attachments labelled at the basiocciput/foramen magnum, atlas, third cervical, and second sacral segments, continuing as the filum terminale. This single inelastic sleeve is the core link.

🩺 Why the S2 attachment is the whole reason the sacrum is in this model

The spinal dura is anchored superiorly at the foramen magnum (occiput) and inferiorly at S2 (sacrum). That single continuous, inelastic tube is the mechanical link that makes the sacrum a midline PRM structure moving in flexion/extension with the occiput, about a superior transverse axis at S2. This is called the core link. Treating the sacrum can therefore be a way of addressing the cranial base, and vice versa.

The named dural folds (the reciprocal tension system in practice)

  • Falx cerebri — vertical, midline; separates the two cerebral hemispheres. Attaches anteriorly to the crista galli of the ethmoid, posteriorly to the internal occipital protuberance.
  • Falx cerebelli — small vertical fold below the tentorium, between the cerebellar hemispheres.
  • Tentorium cerebelli — horizontal, tent-shaped; separates cerebrum above from cerebellum below. Its attachments include the temporal bones, which is the mechanical reason temporal bone dysfunction and membranous strain travel together.
  • Sutherland's fulcrum — the automatically shifting suspension point where the falces and tentorium meet (near the straight sinus). Membranous tension pivots around it; it moves rather than staying fixed.

Q: At which specific levels does the spinal dura have firm attachments, and what is the functional consequence?

Answer

Foramen magnum, C2, C3, and S2. Because the dura is inelastic and firmly fixed at both ends of this span, motion of the occiput at the foramen magnum is mechanically transmitted along the dural tube to the sacrum at S2 — the core link — making the sacrum move involuntarily between the ilia in phase with the cranial mechanism, about a superior transverse axis at S2.

LO 4 — The Five Principles of the PRM

The Core List

The Five Principles (Phenomena) of the Primary Respiratory Mechanism

This is the single most memorizable, most examinable list in the lecture. Their development and function are synchronous and interdependent — no one of them drives the others alone.

1

Motility of the brain and spinal cord

An inherent, slow, pulse-wave-like motion — the "coiling and uncoiling of the central nervous system."

2

Fluctuation of the cerebrospinal fluid

Cerebrospinal fluid moves in a fluctuant, longitudinal flow pattern with a cyclic, pulse-like rhythm.

3

Mobility of the intracranial & intraspinal membranes

The Reciprocal Tension Membrane (RTM) — the dura, whose tension regulates cranial bone motion. Includes the spinal dura.

4

Articular mobility of the cranial bones

Not joint range of motion — a cyclic shape change of the whole cranium in response to the pull of the membranes.

5

Involuntary mobility of the sacrum between the ilia

Sacral flexion/extension about a superior transverse axis at S2, driven through the dural core link.

🔑 Motility vs. mobility — a definition question waiting to happen
  • Motility = the ability to move spontaneously and actively, from within. Used for the brain and spinal cord (principle 1) — the tissue generates its own motion.
  • Mobility = the ability of an object to be moved, from outside. Used for the membranes (principle 3) and the cranial bones (principle 4) — they are moved by something else.

So: the CNS has motility; the membranes, bones, and sacrum have mobility. The wording in the list is deliberate.

Principle 1 — Motility of the brain and spinal cord

  • An inherent, slow, pulse-wave-like motion described as coiling and uncoiling.
  • Inhalation/flexion: the central nervous system coils forward, and shortens and thickens.
  • Exhalation/extension: it uncoils, and lengthens and thins.
  • Embryologic hook: the neural tube grows faster than the surrounding structures and folds; the coiling motion is described as a continuing expression of that developmental pattern.

Principle 2 — Fluctuation of the cerebrospinal fluid

  • Cerebrospinal fluid (the clear fluid in the ventricles and subarachnoid space) does not simply circulate — in this model it fluctuates: a longitudinal, to-and-fro flow pattern with a cyclic, pulse-like rhythm.
  • Sutherland called this the "Tide" — hence the treatment method "directing the tide" (LO 7).
  • Two of the treatment goals below — normalize cerebrospinal fluid fluctuation and eliminate circulatory stasis — sit on this principle.

Slide 9 — the cerebrospinal fluid compartment: choroid plexus, the ventricles and apertures, the subarachnoid space, and the arachnoid granulations draining into the superior sagittal sinus. In the cranial model this fluid does not merely circulate — it fluctuates longitudinally.

Principle 3 — Mobility of the membranes (the RTM)

Covered in full in LO 3. The one-line version: the dura is the only true connective tissue in the cranium, it is inelastic, it is attached to the bones and anchored at the foramen magnum, C2, C3, and S2, and its tension regulates cranial bone movement.

Principle 4 — Articular mobility of the cranial bones

💬 Magoun's warning, quoted in lecture

"Do not look for movement as in other joints of the body! This is merely a resiliency — a combination of slight yielding or suppleness in the articulation plus the flexibility of live and pliant bone." — Harold Magoun, DO, Osteopathy in the Cranial Field

In other words: you are not palpating a hinge. You are palpating a cyclic three-dimensional shape change of the whole cranium, produced by the pull of the reciprocal tension membrane, influenced by the coiling/uncoiling of the central nervous system and the fluctuation of the cerebrospinal fluid.

Bone groupBonesMotion typeAxis
Midline structuresOcciput, sphenoid, ethmoid, vomerFlexion / extensionTransverse axes
Lateral (bilaterally paired) structuresTemporal, parietal, frontal, mandible, facial bonesExternal / internal rotationRoughly anteroposterior axes
🩺 Are the sutures actually fused in an adult?

Willard: less than commonly claimed. The classical demonstration is the "beans in a skull" preparation — a dry skull is filled with dried beans and soaked in water; the swelling beans exert steady internal pressure and pop the sutures apart, producing a disarticulated skull. That this works at all means adult sutures are not the solid bony fusion textbooks often imply — though they do become fairly tight. Before puberty they are unambiguously mobile.

Willard's honest framing: at one end of the spectrum you may be dealing with a bone genuinely floating on a membrane and driven by a vascular rhythm; at the other end, the bones may be effectively locked and you are palpating a vascular rhythm alone. Both are live possibilities.

Principle 5 — Involuntary mobility of the sacrum between the ilia

  • The sacrum is a midline structure, so it flexes and extends rather than rotating.
  • Motion occurs about the superior transverse axis at S2 — the same level as the inferior dural attachment. This axis serves both thoracic respiration and the PRM.
  • PRM inhalation / flexion = COUNTERNUTATION — sacral base posterior, apex anterior.
  • PRM exhalation / extension = NUTATION — sacral base anterior, apex posterior.
  • "Involuntary" is doing work in that phrase: this is not the sacral motion you produce with muscle activity or with a thoracic breath — it is carried passively through the dural core link.

Q: List the five principles of the Primary Respiratory Mechanism, and state for each whether the structure is described as having motility or mobility.

Answer

1. Motility of the brain and spinal cord (moves spontaneously/actively — coils and uncoils). 2. Fluctuation of the cerebrospinal fluid (longitudinal, cyclic). 3. Mobility of the intracranial and intraspinal membranes — the Reciprocal Tension Membrane. 4. Articular mobility of the cranial bones. 5. Involuntary mobility of the sacrum between the ilia. Their development and function are synchronous and interdependent.

LO 5 — Indications & Contraindications for OCMM

Clinical Decision-Making

When to Treat, and When Absolutely Not

⚠️ Learn the contraindications first — this is the safety question

Osteopathic Cranial Manipulative Medicine is generally safe and gentle, which is exactly why the absolute contraindications get tested: the risk is not the force applied, it is treating a head that has something dangerous going on inside it.

🛑

ABSOLUTE Contraindications

  • Patient refusal
  • Acute intracranial bleed or neurological instability
  • Skull fracture
  • Acute cerebrovascular accident (acute stroke)
⚠️

RELATIVE Contraindications

  • Coagulopathy (a bleeding/clotting disorder)
  • Space-occupying lesion in the cranium (e.g. tumor, abscess)
  • Increased intracranial pressure
🔑 Memory hook for the absolutes

"Refuse, Bleed, Break, Stroke" — patient refusal, intracranial bleed/neurologic instability, skull break (fracture), acute stroke. The relatives are the three "pressure and bleeding risk" items: coagulopathy, mass lesion, raised intracranial pressure.

Indications — clinical presentations with relevant somatic dysfunction

Cranial neuropathy / nerve entrapment

Nerve compressed as it exits the skull

Bell's palsy (sudden one-sided weakness of the facial muscles), trigeminal neuralgia (severe stabbing facial pain).

Orofacial pain & jaw

Mouth, face, and jaw mechanics

Temporomandibular joint (TMJ) dysfunction and malocclusion (teeth not meeting correctly).

Infant & pediatric

Feeding, shape, and posture

Colic, feeding difficulties (infant and adult), plagiocephaly (flattening/asymmetry of the skull), torticollis (the neck held twisted to one side).

Head pain & head injury

Chronic and post-traumatic

Headache, post-concussive syndrome, traumatic brain injury — once acute bleeding and fracture are excluded.

Ear, nose & sinus

Drainage and vestibular

Otitis media (middle-ear infection), sinusitis, tinnitus (ringing in the ears), vertigo (spinning sensation).

Goals of treatment — the seven Sendzicki lists

  1. Normalize nerve function — cranial nerves, spinal nerves, and the autonomic nervous system.
  2. Counteract factors producing central nervous system stress — framed as the neuro-endocrine-immune network.
  3. Eliminate circulatory stasis — normalize arterial supply, venous drainage, and lymphatic flow.
  4. Normalize cerebrospinal fluid fluctuation.
  5. Release membranous tension.
  6. Correct or resolve cranial articular strains.
  7. Modify gross structural patterns.

Slides 29–30 — positional (deformational) plagiocephaly before and after Osteopathic Cranial Manipulative Medicine. Top row before, bottom row after: note the reduction in occipital flattening and in the compensatory forward shift of the ear and forehead on the affected side.

🩺 Hospital consult service — where this is actually used (Maine Medical Center)
  • Neonates — nursery and neonatal intensive care unit: feeding disorders, torticollis, positional plagiocephaly (especially preterm), and infants with neonatal abstinence syndrome (withdrawal after in-utero drug exposure).
  • Pediatrics — feeding disorders, sinus and ear infection, palliative care (e.g. brain tumors).
  • Adults — headache of multiple etiologies: after subarachnoid hemorrhage with surgical stabilization, after neurosurgery, after intubation, after delivery, and meningeal or sinus origin headache.

Q: A 34-year-old presents 4 hours after a fall from a ladder with a headache, and imaging shows a non-displaced temporal bone fracture with a small acute epidural hematoma. She asks for cranial treatment for the headache. What do you do?

Answer

Do not perform Osteopathic Cranial Manipulative Medicine. This patient has two absolute contraindications: a skull fracture and an acute intracranial bleed. She also has the relative contraindication of potential increased intracranial pressure. Manage the neurosurgical emergency; cranial treatment may be considered later once the bleed is resolved and she is neurologically stable.

LO 6 — Palpate the CRI Using Three Contacts

Lab · Palpation

The Three Holds: Vault, Base (Becker), and A-P

Exercise #1 in lab is purely experiential — no treatment intent. You try each of three hand positions for 5–7 minutes each, looking for the Cranial Rhythmic Impulse, the articular mobility of the cranium, and the shape change of the head. Sutherland's framing: "the head is a modified sphere" — a three-dimensional shape change occurs across the inhalation/exhalation cycle, not a single-plane movement.

1 · Vault Hold

Manual pg. 25 · fingers spread over the vault

The workhorse diagnostic hold. Used to diagnose cranial dysfunctions, especially cranial base patterns at the sphenobasilar synchondrosis. The hands cradle the vault so that the fingers make contact with the greater wings of the sphenoid, the temporal bones, and the occiput, giving you both sides of the base at once.

2 · Base Hold (Becker Hold)

Manual pg. 26 · both hands cradle the occiput

Both hands cradle the occiput, fingers pointing toward the patient's feet. The fingers may also contact the upper cervical segments and/or the muscular attachments on the inferior portion of the occiput. Good for the occiput–upper cervical relationship and for suboccipital tissue texture.

3 · A-P Hold (Fronto-occipital Hold)

Manual pg. 25 · one hand front, one hand back

Anterior-posterior. Either the occiput is cradled with one hand while the other contacts the frontal bone; or both hands are placed with the fingers pointing toward the feet. Emphasizes the anterior-posterior dimension of the shape change (the diameter that decreases in flexion and increases in extension).

Slide 34 — vault hold finger placements (A–D). This is the figure most likely to be reproduced as a labelling question.

Slide 34 — vault hold demonstrated on a skull model

Slide 35 — base hold (Becker hold)

Slide 36 — A-P hold (fronto-occipital hold): one hand on the frontal bone, the other cradling the occiput.

Vault hold — the four finger contacts, spelled out (A–D)

LetterFingerContact
AIndex fingerOn the greater wing of the sphenoid, just anterior to the pterion (the H-shaped junction of frontal, parietal, temporal, and sphenoid on the side of the skull).
BLong (middle) fingerOn the squamous wing of the temporal bone, just anterior to the external auditory meatus (the ear canal opening).
CRing fingerOn the mastoid process of the temporal bone, just posterior to the auricle (the external ear).
DSmall (little) fingerOn the base of the occiput, just medial to the occipitomastoid suture.

Read the pattern: the index finger is on the sphenoid and the little finger is on the occiput — the two bones of the sphenobasilar synchondrosis — with the two middle fingers spanning the temporal bone between them. That is precisely why this hold is the one used to diagnose cranial base patterns.

🔑 Which hold for which job
  • Vault hold → diagnosing cranial base (SBS) strain patterns. If a stem asks which hold is used to diagnose base patterns, this is the answer.
  • Base / Becker hold → occiput and upper cervical relationship, suboccipital tissues.
  • A-P / fronto-occipital hold → the front-to-back shape change; useful when the frontal bone is of interest.
🧠 What "short rhythm" vs. "long rhythm" palpators taught us

Experienced practitioners historically split into camps — some reported only a long rhythm, some only a short one, and they looked down on each other. When Nelson and Glonek recorded both groups against laser-Doppler flowmetry, the answer was embarrassing and useful: the "long rhythm" people were marking only the peaks of the wave; the "short rhythm" people were marking both the peaks and the troughs — doubling the apparent rate. Same wave, different sampling.

Willard's image: three blind people palpating an elephant — one has the tail, one the leg, one the trunk, and each confidently declares a different animal.

🩺 You can find this rhythm away from the head

The same low-frequency oscillation is recorded and palpated at the sacrum, and some practitioners report feeling it at the feet. The fluid model explains why (see LO 9): the venous plexus involved runs continuously from the cavernous sinus at the cranial base, down the vertebral/epidural (Batson's) plexus around the spinal cord, out through every intervertebral foramen into the paraspinal muscles, and all the way to the pelvic basin.

Q: You want to diagnose a sphenobasilar synchondrosis strain pattern. Which of the three standard holds do you choose, and why?

Answer

The vault hold. It is specifically described as the hold "used to diagnose cranial dysfunctions, especially base patterns," because the finger placement contacts the greater wings of the sphenoid and the occiput simultaneously — the two bones forming the sphenobasilar synchondrosis — letting you sense their relative motion.

LO 7 — Six Principles of Cranial Treatment

Treatment Theory

Principles of Treatment for the Cranium

🔑 The aim of any cranial treatment

Correct cranial somatic dysfunction, normalize function, and release strain.

And the naming distinction that gets tested: cranial strains are MEMBRANOUS articular strains — the restriction lives in the dural membrane. Contrast with the strains you treat elsewhere in the body, which are LIGAMENTOUS articular strains. That is why the cranial balance point is called Balanced Membranous Tension and the peripheral one is called Balanced Ligamentous Tension.

#MethodWhat you doDirect or indirect?
aBalanced Membranous Tension (BMT)Carry the articulation to the point where the membranes are poised between normal free-range tension and the increased tension that precedes the strain; hold and let the inherent forces resolve it.Balance point (neither)
bExaggerationCarry the dysfunction further into its position of ease — away from the restriction — then allow release.Indirect
cDirecting the TideUse the fluid itself as the corrective force: direct the cerebrospinal fluid fluctuation toward the restricted area from a distant contact point.Fluid-directed
dDirect ActionEngage the restrictive barrier and carry the dysfunction toward the restriction.Direct
eDisengagementTraction/separation — gently pull the articular surfaces apart to free an impacted or jammed suture.Direct (separation)
fOpposite Physiologic MotionMove the structure in the direction opposite to its normal physiologic motion to free the restriction.Direct
💬 The formal definition of Balanced Membranous Tension (learn this wording)

"Balanced Membranous Tension may be defined as the point in the range of motion of an articulation where the membranes are poised between the normal tension present throughout the free range and the increased tension preceding the strain or fixation which occurs as a joint is carried beyond its physiological range."

Magoun adds, in Osteopathy in the Cranial Field: "Finding it tests the palpatory skill and power of concentration of the cranial student."

Note the scope: Balanced Membranous Tension refers to the Reciprocal Tension Membrane (the dura) and is used to treat the articulations of the cranium, face, and sacrum.

🧠 How to tell direct from indirect at a glance
  • Indirect = move away from the restriction, toward ease. Here: exaggeration.
  • Direct = move into the restriction, engaging the barrier. Here: direct action, disengagement, opposite physiologic motion.
  • Neither / balance point = find the poised midpoint and wait. Here: balanced membranous tension.
  • Fluid = the corrective force is the cerebrospinal fluid, not your positioning. Here: directing the tide.

Q: A physician places two fingers on either side of a restricted suture and applies gentle traction to separate the articular surfaces, while the other hand's fingers rest on the contralateral skull at the point of greatest distance to send fluid toward the restriction. Which two treatment principles are being combined?

Answer

Disengagement (the gentle traction separating the suture) combined with directing the tide / directing fluid (the contralateral hand). This combination is the V-spread technique — see LO 8.

LO 8 — Perform the OCMM Techniques

Lab · Technique

The Four Techniques: Condylar Decompression, OA Release, V-Spread, CV4

Practice in lab: condylar decompression and the occipito-atlantal (OA) balanced ligamentous tension release. Discuss but do not practice: V-spread and CV4.

Exercise #2 · Manual pg. 32

Condylar Decompression Technique

The problem being addressed: a condylar compression dysfunction — the condylar parts of the occiput are compressed against or converged on the facets of the atlas, often with an associated strain pattern between the condylar parts and the occipital squama. In a neonate this can follow the compressive forces of birth.

Slide 37 — condylar compression dysfunction. Left: ideal structure, opisthion centred. Right: a possible strain pattern — opisthion deviated toward the right, with the condylar parts acting as pincers on the foramen magnum. The technique below opens those pincers.

  1. Position
    Neonate supine; physician seated at the baby's head, cradling the head in two hands. Adult variation: the patient is asked to tuck the chin, which draws the occipital condyles posteriorly and out of anterior convergence on the facets of the atlas.
  2. Contact
    Cradle the occiput with the palms. Place the index or middle fingers on the condylar parts, as close to them as possible. Start with the elbows in a widened position.
  3. The action — think caliper
    Slowly draw the elbows toward one another. Because of the geometry, this widens the finger contact on the condylar parts, drawing them laterally apart — decompressing them. (Elbows in → fingers out.)
  4. Endpoint — infants
    Treatment is complete when the position of the condylar parts is more physiologic and the cranial base strain has improved.
  5. Endpoint — adults
    Treatment is complete when there is softening or change in tissue texture, or improved freedom of motion between the occiput and the atlas.

Slide 38 — condylar decompression in a neonate: palms cradle the occiput, index/middle fingers reach the condylar parts, elbows start wide and are drawn together.

⚠️ The counterintuitive bit that gets tested

Elbows move toward each other; the fingers move apart. Students often describe it backwards. It works like a caliper: closing the handles opens the jaws.

Exercise #3 · Manual pg. 34

Occipito-atlantal (OA) Release — a Balanced Ligamentous Tension technique

Slide 39 — the contact point: posterior tubercle of C1

Slide 39 — suboccipital layer and the posterior atlanto-occipital membrane

  1. Patient tucks the chin. This releases the anterior convergence on the facets of the atlas — the same mechanical goal as in the adult condylar decompression setup.
  2. Contact the posterior tubercle of C1 with the pad of a finger.
  3. Balance side-slipping — find the point of balanced tension in the side-to-side (translatory) motion at the joint.
  4. Use inhalation for respiratory cooperation to obtain the release at the occipito-atlantal joint. (Respiratory cooperation = asking the patient to breathe in a way that adds an inherent force to your balance point — a standard Balanced Ligamentous Tension activating force.)

V-Spread Technique Manual pg. 27 discuss only

Purpose: performed to free a sutural restriction or dysfunction. A classic traumatic example is a baseball to the ear driving a suture into restriction.

Mechanism: it is a combination of disengagement and directing fluid.

  • Treating hand: two fingers placed on either side of the suture to be released, forming a "V"; gentle traction is exerted to disengage the suture.
  • Opposite hand: one or two fingers placed at the point of greatest distance on the contralateral side of the skull. The intent is to direct fluid to the restricted suture to facilitate softening or release.
🩺 The example you should be able to reproduce

At the occipitomastoid (OM) suture — where the occiput meets the mastoid part of the temporal bone. This suture forms a wall of the jugular foramen. Relieving resistance and disengaging the OM suture releases entrapment at the jugular foramen and therefore affects the structures passing through it: the glossopharyngeal (CN IX), vagus (CN X), and spinal accessory (CN XI) nerves.

CV4 — Compression of the Fourth Ventricle Manual pg. 30 discuss only

A technique for the management of cerebrospinal fluid fluctuation. The operator's thenar eminences contact the occipital squama medial to the occipitomastoid sutures; the occiput is held in extension and resisted through successive cycles until the rhythm quiets to a still point, then is released.

⚠️ Willard's caveat about the name

Willard — who does small-animal surgery — points out that the floor of the fourth ventricle is the one place you never want to touch: in an animal, contact there produces one or two gasps and death, because the medullary respiratory and cardiovascular centers sit there. He is not saying the technique does nothing (the flowmetry data shows it clearly does something reproducible). He is saying the label is a hypothesis, not a description of the mechanism — an excellent illustration of the data-vs-hypothesis theme.

Q: A patient has hoarseness and difficulty swallowing after head trauma. You find a restricted occipitomastoid suture. Which technique is indicated, which foramen is involved, and which cranial nerves are at risk?

Answer

V-spread at the occipitomastoid suture — a combination of disengagement (two fingers straddling the suture with gentle traction) and directing fluid (contralateral hand at the point of greatest distance). The occipitomastoid suture forms a wall of the jugular foramen, through which pass the glossopharyngeal (CN IX), vagus (CN X), and spinal accessory (CN XI) nerves. Hoarseness and dysphagia point at vagus and glossopharyngeal involvement.

9 — Evidence: What the Recordings Actually Show

Willard · Research

Data vs. Hypothesis: Can a Human Palpate — and Change — This Rhythm?

Willard's lecture answers three sequential questions with recorded data. Learn them as a chain, because that is how they are likely to be tested.

1

Does a rhythm exist?

Yes. Laser-Doppler flowmetry plus Fourier analysis reliably shows four cardiovascular waves, including a 5–8 cycles/minute baroreflex (Traube-Hering-Mayer) wave.

2

Can a human palpate it?

Yes. Blinded examiners' event marks track the peaks of that wave — including its amplitude and frequency modulation — with a consistent, explainable small lag.

3

Can a human change it?

Yes. Both sham contact and real treatment change the power in that band — in opposite directions.

The palpation experiment — why the design matters

  1. Setup
    A volunteer lies supine. A skilled examiner sits at the head and takes a hold. A laser-Doppler probe records cutaneous blood-flow velocity continuously.
  2. The blinding
    The technician with the computer sits away from the table. The examiner cannot see the tracing — and even if they could, the raw record is dominated by cardiac chatter and is unreadable in real time. There is no way to know where you are in the cycle.
  3. The task
    The examiner calls out the event they feel ("flexion," or simply "now"). The question deliberately is not "what is flexion?" but "when do you feel the event?" The technician presses a key, dropping an event marker onto the record.
  4. The result
    Markers land just off the peaks of the 5–8 cycles/minute wave, offset by a consistent amount — which was calculated to equal the time to palpate it, think it, say it, hear it, and press the key. Thousands of recordings; not a one-off.
  5. The finding Willard calls stunning
    The wave being followed is both amplitude-modulated and frequency-modulated, and examiners tracked it through those modulations — including reporting "I'm losing it" precisely where the amplitude collapsed (the still point) and picking it back up when it returned.

Sham contact vs. real treatment — opposite effects

🚫

Mock palpation (rocking fingers on the temporal bone)

  • Power in the baroreflex band shot UP, consistently.
  • It was then held up — a sustained elevation.
  • Willard's reading: this is the wrong direction. Raising and pinning sympathetically-driven vascular tone is what you are trying not to do.
  • A loud noise in the room produced the same spike — a startle response, further evidence the band is sympathetically driven.
✅

Real treatment (CV4 by a skilled practitioner)

  • Power in the baroreflex band DROPPED during the technique — slowed and slowed until it effectively disappeared. That is the operator's still point.
  • On release, everything surged upward in a large burst, then tapered back down about as fast as it rose.
  • Subtracting the pre-treatment from the treatment spectrum shows the change is specific to the baroreflex band.
  • Net effect: variability is injected into the system — the opposite of pinning it.
🔑 Why "injecting variability" is the clinically meaningful part

A consistent, non-variable heart rate is a bad sign, not a good one. Loss of heart rate variability means the autonomic system — usually the sympathetic side — has pinned the rate against a wall and is holding it there without room to respond. Reduced heart rate variability is a well-established marker in depression and is strongly linked to cardiovascular disease (Musselman, Evans & Nemeroff, Arch Gen Psychiatry 1998). Restoring variability has been associated with better outcomes and longevity.

So the interesting claim is not "cranial treatment moves bones." It is: a manual technique produced a reproducible, band-specific change that added variability back into an autonomic control loop.

Two competing models for what your hands are on

💧

Model A — Fluid dynamics (Willard's preferred candidate)

What you feel is pulsation in tissue from perfusion, within a very dense venous system.

  • The skull is surrounded by dense vasculature — the occipital sinus in particular is often packed with veins (which is why it is commonly found full of clot on dissection).
  • This is continuous with the vertebral/epidural venous plexus (Batson's plexus), which wraps the spinal cord, exits at every intervertebral foramen, and continues into the paraspinal muscles.
  • It runs from the cavernous sinus at the cranial base to the pelvic basin — explaining why the rhythm is palpable at the head, sacrum, and even the feet.
  • It also explains the CV4 tracing: tightening the hold could evacuate the plexus; releasing lets it refill abruptly, producing exactly the observed burst-then-taper. (Willard flags this as informed speculation, not established fact.)
🦴

Model B — Moving bones (the classical model)

What you feel is the articular mobility of the cranial bones themselves — Sutherland's original framing and what you are taught to palpate.

  • Straightforward before puberty, when sutures are clearly mobile.
  • After puberty sutures tighten but are not as fused as usually portrayed — the beans-in-a-skull demonstration pops them apart with modest steady pressure.
  • Plausible spectrum: at one end, a bone genuinely floating on membrane and driven by the vascular rhythm; at the other end, bones effectively locked, so you are palpating only a vascular rhythm.
💬 The moment worth remembering

Willard told Kenneth Nelson, who ran the Osteopathic Manipulative Medicine program in Chicago and produced this data, that it was great because "now you can re-evaluate the models" — and mentioned the moving-bone model. Nelson, in Willard's telling, "totally exploded." That reaction is the data-vs-hypothesis lesson: the data substantiates a great deal, and it may also require readjusting the story that has been built on top of it.

The clinical trial evidence — recurrent otitis media

🧠 Why the ear is the natural test case

In an infant, the face has not yet expanded and the eustachian tube (which drains the middle ear into the pharynx) is relatively flat/horizontal — poor gravity drainage, so middle-ear fluid sits and gets infected. As the face grows, the tube angles downward; this really takes hold around 6 years of age, which is precisely when recurrent otitis media stops being a major problem. A mechanical, developmental, drainage problem is exactly the kind of thing a structural intervention might plausibly influence.

StudyYear & JournalInterventionConclusion
Paradise et al.2001 · New England Journal of MedicinePrompt vs. delayed tympanostomy tubes (ear tubes) for persistent otitis mediaIn children under 3 with persistent otitis media, prompt tube insertion does not measurably improve developmental outcomes at age 3.
Paradise et al.2005 · New England Journal of MedicineSame cohort, longer follow-upPrompt tube insertion does not improve developmental outcomes at age 6.
Paradise et al.2007 · New England Journal of MedicineSame cohort, longest follow-upPrompt tube insertion does not improve developmental outcomes at ages 9–11.
Mills et al.2003 · Archives of Pediatrics & Adolescent MedicineOsteopathic manipulative treatment as adjuvant therapy in children with recurrent acute otitis media (randomized controlled trial)Fewer episodes of otitis media, fewer surgical procedures, more surgery-free months, and children were more likely to have normal tympanograms, compared with usual care.

Slide 40 — Mills et al., 2003: objective and study design. Note the enrolment criteria (6 months to 6 years old, 3 episodes of acute otitis media in the previous 6 months or 4 in the previous year, not already surgical candidates) and the double blinding — the pediatrician was blinded to group and outcomes, the osteopathic physician to clinical course.

Slide 40 — Mills et al., 2003: results. 57 patients (25 intervention, 32 control). Fewer episodes of acute otitis media (P = .04), fewer surgical procedures — 1 vs. 8 (P = .03), more surgery-free months (6.00 vs. 5.25; P = .01), more normal tympanogram types (P = .02), and no adverse reactions.

🩺 Details of the Mills trial that make it worth knowing
  • Led by Miriam Mills (Oklahoma), with stringent enrollment criteria for children with recurrent acute otitis media.
  • The protocol was deliberately not scripted. Physicians were told to palpate and treat the patient as they would normally — "do whatever you think you need to do to help the child." The question tested was therefore "does the osteopathic approach work?", not "does this one hand placement work?"
  • Outcomes monitored: drug use, surgery, and tympanograms (a test of eardrum mobility and middle-ear pressure). Tympanograms had been dulled by middle-ear pressure and measurably improved.
  • The editor of the journal, Ed Klein — the world authority on otitis media and author of the standard textbook — did not trust the result and had the journal's own statisticians redo the analysis. The finding held. Power was low and recruitment difficult, but statistically it was there.
  • Klein's published editorial: recurrent otitis media is extremely common and managed daily; no current treatment option is impressively effective or free of complications; osteopathic manipulation is "an intriguing potential addition to the care of this common chronic problem."

Willard's framing model: homeostasis, allostasis, and allostatic load

ConceptRegulationSet point?
HomeostasisFeedback regulation — the system senses a deviation and corrects itYes
AllostasisFeedforward regulation — the system anticipates demand and changes the operating rangeNo
  • Allostatic load = the cumulative effects of repeated bouts of allostatic activation (McEwen, New England Journal of Medicine, 1998). The bill that comes due for chronically running the body outside its resting range.
  • The allostatic index — the measured panel: blood pressure, waist-to-hip ratio, high-density lipoprotein (HDL) and total cholesterol, glycosylated hemoglobin (HbA1c), urinary norepinephrine and epinephrine, and cortisol.
  • In Willard's whole-host diagram, homeostatic rhythms sit alongside the arousal system, the neuro-endocrine-immune network, genetic factors, and structural/psychosocial/medical factors, all feeding allostatic load, which combines with disease to produce illness. This is where palpable rhythms connect to the wider osteopathic model.

Q: In the Nelson and Glonek laser-Doppler experiments, what happened to the power of the Traube-Hering-Mayer band during (a) sham rocking of the fingers on the temporal bone and (b) an actual CV4 technique, and what happened on release?

Answer

(a) Sham/mock palpation: the baroreflex band power INCREASED and was held elevated — the same response a startling noise in the room produced, consistent with a sympathetic arousal effect, and the opposite of the therapeutic goal. (b) Real CV4: the band power DECREASED, slowing until the rhythm effectively stopped — the still point. On release, activity surged in a large burst and then tapered back down about as quickly, injecting variability into the system. Loss of variability (as in depression and cardiovascular disease) is the pathologic state; restoring it is the plausible benefit.

Reference

Board Pearls — Anatomy Is the Answer

🔑 The general rule Sendzicki gives for cranial board questions

Relate the clinical problem to head and neck anatomy. Ask: which bone? which suture? which foramen? which nerve passes through it? Most "cranial" board questions are anatomy questions wearing a cranial costume.

PresentationThink · Bone / StructureNerve or mechanism
Facial nerve palsy (Bell's palsy) — sudden, unilateral, peripheral; ~50% idiopathicTemporal boneFacial nerve (CN VII) — traverses the temporal bone via the internal acoustic meatus and facial canal, exiting at the stylomastoid foramen
Vertigo (spinning sensation)Temporal bone dysfunctionVestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) — vestibular apparatus is housed in the petrous temporal bone
Hoarseness, dysphagia, shoulder weakness after head traumaOccipitomastoid (OM) suture → forms a wall of the jugular foramenGlossopharyngeal (CN IX), vagus (CN X), spinal accessory (CN XI) — treat with V-spread
Trigeminal neuralgia — severe stabbing facial painTemporal bone / tentorium cerebelli (Meckel's cave sits on the petrous ridge)Trigeminal nerve (CN V)
Recurrent otitis media in a child under 6Temporal bone and the developing faceFlat eustachian tube → poor drainage; angles down by ~age 6
Sympathetic / parasympathetic balance questionThink anatomy: where do the fibers run?Vagus (CN X) through the jugular foramen for parasympathetic; cervical sympathetic chain and the sympathoadrenal baroreflex band for sympathetic
🩺 Pediatric indications you should recognize on sight
  • Recurrent otitis media — the Mills 2003 trial is the supporting evidence.
  • Feeding disorders in neonates and preterm infants — a hospital consult mainstay.
  • Positional plagiocephaly — asymmetric skull flattening from sustained positioning, common in premature infants; before/after treatment photographs are shown in lecture.
  • Torticollis — the neck held twisted to one side.
  • Neonatal abstinence syndrome — infants withdrawing after in-utero drug exposure.

Glossary — Every Abbreviation and Opaque Term in This Lecture

Term / AbbreviationFull formPlain-language meaning
OCMMOsteopathic Cranial Manipulative MedicineHands-on treatment applied to the head, face, and sacrum using the cranial model.
OCFOsteopathy in the Cranial FieldThe older name for the same field; also the title of Magoun's 1951 textbook.
OMTOsteopathic Manipulative TreatmentHands-on osteopathic treatment generally.
PRMPrimary Respiratory MechanismThe five-component model of inherent cyclic motion in the body.
CRICranial Rhythmic ImpulseThe palpable rhythm the PRM produces; 10–14 cycles/minute in a healthy adult.
RTMReciprocal Tension MembraneThe dural membrane system whose tension regulates cranial bone movement.
CNSCentral nervous systemBrain and spinal cord.
CSFCerebrospinal fluidThe clear fluid bathing the brain and spinal cord.
SBSSphenobasilar synchondrosisThe cartilaginous junction of the sphenoid body and the basilar occiput; the reference joint for cranial base patterns.
BMTBalanced Membranous TensionThe poised midpoint in a cranial articulation's range where the membranes balance.
BLTBalanced Ligamentous TensionThe equivalent balance-point technique used elsewhere in the body.
CV4Compression of the Fourth VentricleA fluid technique using occipital contact to induce a still point.
OAOccipito-atlantal jointWhere the occipital condyles meet the atlas (C1).
OM sutureOccipitomastoid sutureOcciput meets mastoid part of temporal bone; forms a wall of the jugular foramen.
THMTraube-Hering-Mayer oscillationThe 5–8 cycles/minute baroreflex blood-flow wave; linked by flowmetry studies to what palpators call the CRI.
cps / cpmCycles per second / cycles per minuteUnits of frequency. 1 cps = 60 cpm.
Motility—The ability to move spontaneously and actively, from within (used for the CNS).
Mobility—The ability to be moved by something else (used for membranes, bones, sacrum).
Nutation—Sacral base moves anterior, apex posterior. In the PRM this is exhalation/extension.
Counternutation—Sacral base moves posterior, apex anterior. In the PRM this is inhalation/flexion.
Still point—An interval where the rhythm's amplitude drops below the palpable threshold and seems to stop; the therapeutic endpoint of CV4.
Core link—The dural connection from foramen magnum to S2 that mechanically couples occiput and sacrum.
Sutherland's fulcrum—The automatically shifting suspension point of the dural membrane system, near the straight sinus.
Falx cerebri / cerebelli—Vertical midline dural folds separating the cerebral hemispheres / cerebellar hemispheres.
Tentorium cerebelli—Horizontal, tent-shaped dural fold separating cerebrum from cerebellum; attaches to the temporal bones.
Plagiocephaly—Asymmetric flattening of the skull, commonly from sustained positioning.
Torticollis—The neck held persistently twisted/tilted to one side.
Malocclusion—Upper and lower teeth do not meet correctly.
TMJTemporomandibular jointThe jaw joint, just in front of the ear.
Tympanogram—A test of eardrum mobility and middle-ear pressure; abnormal ("dulled") with middle-ear effusion.
Tympanostomy tubes—"Ear tubes" — small tubes surgically placed through the eardrum to drain and ventilate the middle ear.
Otitis media—Middle-ear infection.
Eustachian tube—The tube draining the middle ear into the pharynx; flat in infants, angles downward by about age 6.
Coagulopathy—A disorder of blood clotting — bleeds too easily.
CVACerebrovascular accidentStroke.
ICPIntracranial pressurePressure inside the skull; raised pressure is dangerous.
NICUNeonatal intensive care unitIntensive care for newborns.
NASNeonatal abstinence syndromeWithdrawal in a newborn after in-utero drug exposure.
TBITraumatic brain injuryBrain injury from external force.
SAHSubarachnoid hemorrhageBleeding into the space around the brain.
Laser-Doppler flowmetry—A skin-clip device that measures blood-flow velocity in capillaries using a laser beam.
Fourier transformation—A mathematical conversion of a time-based recording into a frequency-based one, producing a power spectrum.
Power spectrum—A graph where x = frequency (events per second) and y = energy present at that frequency.
Amplitude / frequency—Amplitude = how far a wave swings from midline (energy). Frequency = how often the wave repeats.
Boundary condition—The physical limit that reverses an oscillation at each end of its swing.
Baroreflex—The blood-pressure feedback loop: baroreceptors sense pressure, autonomic output adjusts heart rate and vessel tone.
HRVHeart rate variabilityBeat-to-beat variation in heart rate. More variability is healthier; loss of it accompanies depression and cardiovascular disease.
Homeostasis—Feedback regulation around a set point.
Allostasis—Feedforward regulation with no set point — anticipating demand and shifting the operating range.
Allostatic load—The cumulative wear from repeated allostatic activation (McEwen, 1998).
HbA1cGlycosylated hemoglobinA blood test reflecting average glucose over ~3 months; part of the allostatic index.
HDLHigh-density lipoproteinThe "good" cholesterol carrier; part of the allostatic index.
Batson's plexusVertebral (epidural) venous plexusA valveless venous network from the cavernous sinus to the pelvis, wrapping the spinal cord — the anatomic basis of the fluid model.
Gap junction—A direct cytoplasmic bridge between two cells — the structure that made both Golgi and Cajal partly right.

🎯 Osteopathy in the Cranial Field — High-Yield One-Pager

LO1 Biorhythms · LO2 PRM · LO3 RTM · LO4 Five Principles · LO5 Indications/Contraindications · LO6 Holds · LO7 Treatment Principles · LO8 Techniques · Evidence

LO 1 · BIORHYTHMS

The three you must distinguish

  • Heart rate: ~60/min · ~0.9 cycles per second
  • Diaphragmatic respiration: 12–18/min · 0.2–0.3 cps
  • Cranial Rhythmic Impulse (CRI): 10–14/min healthy adult

Four long cardiovascular waves (laser-Doppler)

  • 0.9 cps (~60/min) — cardiac
  • 0.2–0.3 cps (12–18/min) — respiratory
  • 0.1 cps (5–8/min) — baroreflex = Traube-Hering-Mayer ← what palpators track
  • 0.02–0.05 cps (<1/min) — thermal / renin-angiotensin

CRI rate changes

  • Faster: fever, vigorous exercise, after OMT to the PRM
  • Slower: depression, stress (physical/emotional), chronic fatigue, chronic infection

Power spectrum — don't misread it

  • x-axis = frequency (events/sec), NOT time
  • y-axis = power (energy at that frequency)
  • Made by Fourier transformation of a laser-Doppler tracing
  • Still point = superimposed waves cancel; amplitude drops below palpable threshold
LO 2 · PRM

Definition & phases

  • PRM = 5 integrated anatomic-physiologic components, synchronous & interdependent. Sutherland (1873–1954), The Cranial Bowl, 1939
  • PRM = mechanism; CRI = the palpable rhythm it produces
  • INHALATION = flexion + external rotation. SBS rises, vault lowers, A-P diameter decreases, skull widens. CNS coils/shortens/thickens. Sacrum COUNTERnutates (base posterior)
  • EXHALATION = extension + internal rotation. SBS falls, vault rises, A-P increases, skull narrows. CNS uncoils/lengthens/thins. Sacrum NUTATES (base anterior)
  • Midline (flex/extend): occiput, sphenoid, ethmoid, vomer
  • Paired (int/ext rotate): temporal, parietal, frontal, mandible, facial
LO 3 · RTM

Reciprocal Tension Membrane

  • = intracranial + intraspinal membranes; dural tension regulates cranial bone movement
  • Meninges = dura, arachnoid, pia
  • Dura is the only true connective tissue in the cranium
  • 2 layers; outer continuous with inner periosteum & with outer periosteum through sutures → each bone in a membranous bag
  • Layers inseparable except where they split to form venous sinuses
  • Attachments: foramen magnum, C2, C3, S2 → the core link to the sacrum
  • Folds: falx cerebri, falx cerebelli, tentorium cerebelli (attaches temporal bones); Sutherland's fulcrum
LO 4 · FIVE PRINCIPLES

The list (memorize in order)

  • 1. Motility of the brain & spinal cord — coiling/uncoiling
  • 2. Fluctuation of the cerebrospinal fluid — longitudinal, cyclic
  • 3. Mobility of intracranial & intraspinal membranes (RTM)
  • 4. Articular mobility of the cranial bones
  • 5. Involuntary mobility of the sacrum between the ilia

Motility vs. mobility

  • Motility = moves spontaneously & actively (CNS)
  • Mobility = able to be moved (membranes, bones, sacrum)

Magoun on cranial bone motion

  • Not joint movement — a resiliency: slight yielding/suppleness plus flexibility of live, pliant bone
  • Sacral axis = superior transverse axis at S2
LO 5 · INDICATIONS & CONTRAINDICATIONS

ABSOLUTE contraindications — "Refuse, Bleed, Break, Stroke"

  • Patient refusal
  • Acute intracranial bleed / neurologic instability
  • Skull fracture
  • Acute cerebrovascular accident (stroke)

RELATIVE contraindications

  • Coagulopathy
  • Space-occupying cranial lesion
  • Increased intracranial pressure

Indications

  • Cranial neuropathy / entrapment: Bell's palsy, trigeminal neuralgia
  • Orofacial pain, TMJ dysfunction, malocclusion
  • Colic, feeding difficulties, plagiocephaly, torticollis
  • Headache, post-concussive syndrome / traumatic brain injury
  • Otitis media, sinusitis, tinnitus, vertigo

7 goals of treatment

  • Normalize nerve function (cranial, spinal, autonomic)
  • Counteract CNS stress factors (neuro-endocrine-immune)
  • Eliminate circulatory stasis (arterial, venous, lymphatic)
  • Normalize CSF fluctuation
  • Release membranous tension
  • Correct cranial articular strains
  • Modify gross structural patterns
LO 6 · THE THREE HOLDS

5–7 minutes each

  • Vault hold (pg. 25) — diagnoses cranial dysfunction, especially BASE patterns at the SBS
  • Base / Becker hold (pg. 26) — both hands cradle occiput, fingers toward the feet; may contact upper cervical segments and inferior occipital muscle attachments
  • A-P / fronto-occipital hold (pg. 25) — occiput in one hand, other on frontal; or both hands fingers toward feet
  • "The head is a modified sphere" — 3-D shape change
LO 7 · TREATMENT PRINCIPLES

The six methods

  • a. Balanced Membranous Tension — balance point
  • b. Exaggeration — INDIRECT
  • c. Directing the Tide — fluid-driven
  • d. Direct Action — DIRECT
  • e. Disengagement — traction/separation
  • f. Opposite Physiologic Motion

Key distinctions

  • Cranial strains = MEMBRANOUS articular strains (vs. LIGAMENTOUS elsewhere)
  • BMT = point where membranes are poised between normal free-range tension and the increased tension preceding strain/fixation
  • BMT applies to cranium, face, and sacrum
  • Aim: correct somatic dysfunction, normalize function, release strain
LO 8 · TECHNIQUES

Condylar decompression (pg. 32)

  • Palms cradle occiput; index/middle fingers on condylar parts; elbows start wide
  • Draw elbows TOWARD each other like a caliper → fingers spread condylar parts LATERALLY apart
  • Adult: tuck chin to draw condyles posteriorly out of anterior convergence on atlas facets
  • Endpoint — infant: more physiologic position; adult: tissue texture softening or freer occiput-atlas motion

OA release — BLT (pg. 34)

  • Patient tucks chin → releases anterior convergence on atlas facets
  • Contact posterior tubercle of C1 with finger pad
  • Balance side-slipping; use inhalation for respiratory cooperation

V-spread (pg. 27) — discuss only

  • Frees a sutural restriction; = disengagement + directing fluid
  • Two fingers straddle the suture with gentle traction; opposite hand at point of greatest distance contralaterally
  • OM suture → jugular foramen → CN IX (glossopharyngeal), X (vagus), XI (spinal accessory)

CV4 (pg. 30) — discuss only

  • = Compression of the Fourth Ventricle; manages CSF fluctuation; endpoint = still point

Master Reference — Evidence, Board Anatomy, and the Numbers

ItemKey factWhy it matters / what gets asked
Data vs. hypothesisData = objective, replicable observation. Hypothesis = the story built on it. Golgi vs. Cajal (1906 Nobel): same slides, opposite conclusions; gap junctions later showed both were partly right.The framing idea of the whole week — a rhythm exists (data); "moving bones" is one explanation (hypothesis).
Laser-Doppler flowmetrySkin clip (earlobe); detects red-cell compaction (systole) and rarefaction (diastole) in capillaries.How the rhythms were recorded objectively.
Fourier / power spectrumx = frequency (events/sec); y = power (energy). Peak height ≠ beat size.Classic misread — the x-axis is not time.
Nelson, Sergueef, Lipinski, Chapman & Glonek 2001 (JAOA 101:163)CRI related to the Traube-Hering-Mayer oscillation; laser-Doppler vs. palpation. Blinded examiners' event marks fall just off the peaks of the 5–8/min wave; the lag = palpate→think→say→hear→keypress.Evidence a human can palpate a real, amplitude- and frequency-modulated wave.
"Short" vs. "long" rhythm palpatorsLong-rhythm people marked peaks only; short-rhythm people marked peaks AND troughs of the same wave.Same wave, different sampling — the blind-men-and-the-elephant point.
Nelson, Sergueef & Glonek 2006 (JMPT 29:626)Mock palpation (finger rocking) → baroreflex power UP and held up (same as a startling noise). Real CV4 → power DOWN to a still point; on release, a large burst then rapid taper.Sham and real treatment move the same band in opposite directions; treatment adds variability.
Heart rate variabilityFlat, non-variable rate = autonomically pinned = pathologic. Reduced variability accompanies depression and cardiovascular disease (Musselman, Evans & Nemeroff, Arch Gen Psychiatry 1998).Why "injecting variability" is the plausible therapeutic benefit.
Fluid modelDense venous vasculature: occipital sinus → vertebral/epidural (Batson's) plexus → paraspinal muscles; cavernous sinus to pelvic basin.Explains palpability at sacrum and feet, and the CV4 evacuate-then-refill burst.
Bone modelSutures not as fused as portrayed — the beans-in-a-skull demonstration pops them apart. Spectrum: bone floating on membrane ↔ bones locked, vascular rhythm only.Willard's honest "both are possible" position.
Paradise 2001 / 2005 / 2007 (NEJM)Prompt tympanostomy tubes for persistent otitis media do NOT improve developmental outcomes — at age 3, at age 6, or at ages 9–11.The comparator: standard surgical care lacks developmental benefit.
Mills et al. 2003 (Arch Pediatr Adolesc Med 157:861)Randomized controlled trial, OMT as adjuvant in recurrent acute otitis media, unscripted ("treat as you would treat"): fewer episodes, fewer surgical procedures, more surgery-free months, more normal tympanograms. Editor Ed Klein had the statistics redone — the result held.The strongest clinical-trial support cited for cranial treatment.
Eustachian tube developmentFlat/horizontal in infants (poor drainage); angles downward by ~age 6, when recurrent otitis media stops being a major issue.The mechanical rationale for treating the ear structurally.
Homeostasis vs. allostasisHomeostasis = feedback regulation with a set point. Allostasis = feedforward, no set point. Allostatic load = cumulative effect of repeated allostatic activation (McEwen, NEJM 1998).Willard's framing model for where rhythms sit in osteopathic theory.
Allostatic indexBlood pressure · waist-hip ratio · HDL and cholesterol · glycosylated hemoglobin (HbA1c) · urinary norepinephrine & epinephrine · cortisol.Six measurable components — a list question.
Bell's palsySudden unilateral peripheral facial nerve palsy; ~50% idiopathic → think temporal bone, facial nerve (CN VII).Board pearl.
VertigoTemporal bone dysfunction with the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII).Board pearl.
Occipitomastoid sutureOcciput + temporal; forms a wall of the jugular foramen → CN IX, X, XI. Treat with V-spread.Board pearl — the most-tested cranial anatomy link.
Sacral motion trapPRM inhalation/flexion = COUNTERnutation (base posterior). PRM exhalation/extension = nutation (base anterior). Opposite to the postural/respiratory naming convention.Highest-yield single confusable fact in the lecture.
